segments.voice: Yesterday closed reading the Gita's first chapter: Arjuna sitting down, and a chapter named for despair. Now a smaller text, and an old friend from year one.

Two people read the same short text message, and one hears warmth while the other hears a fight. Same letters, two tones. The Isha's opening line has a word like that, and readers have been hearing it two ways for a long time. Isha vasyam idam sarvam yat kim cha jagatyam jagat. Back in year one it came in English. In its own letters, one word, vasyam, can mean dwelt in, or it can mean clothed. So does God live in it all, or clothe it? Two good answers, and they get to speak.
screen: `ONE TEXT, TWO TONES.` → `VASYAM: DWELT IN, OR CLOTHED?` → `TWO ANSWERS SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Start with isha. The stem is ish, the one who rules, the Lord, and this ending means by: by the Lord. Sanskrit puts by into the ending, so one word carries a phrase. Then vasyam, something to be dwelt in, or to be clothed. Here's the first voice. All this is to be dwelt in by the Lord. The world is a house with someone home. Every moving thing has the Lord living inside it, so nothing is empty and nothing is just stuff. Here's the second voice, the one Shankara, the old commentator, takes. All this is to be clothed by the Lord. Wrap everything in the Lord, the way you'd throw a shawl over a chair, so that when you look, you see the shawl first. On this reading the line is a way of seeing, and a practice. The rest of the line names what's being lived in, or wrapped: idam sarvam, all this, and yat kim cha jagatyam jagat, whatever moves in the moving world. Jagat is what moves. Jagatyam is its near twin with an ending that means in. The line names the thing and the place it moves, twice over. The Sanskrit keeps vasyam open, and readers still choose.
screen: `ISHA: BY THE LORD.` · `VOICE ONE: DWELT IN.` · `VOICE TWO: CLOTHED.` · `JAGATYAM JAGAT: THE MOVING, MOVING.`

segments.voice: Say the line out loud, softly, one word to each slow out-breath: isha, vasyam, idam, sarvam, yat, kim, cha, jagatyam, jagat. Then let the words go and listen to whatever moves: the breath, a sound outside, the next thought arriving.
Reading the Isha in the original, from its first word: isha, by the Lord, and vasyam, dwelt in or clothed. One word, two readings, both kept.

notes: First day of the Isha block (1487–1498) in Sanskrit for readers. Year one (days 232–238) taught the meaning; this block reads the grammar and sound, and points back once ('back in year one').

Debate shape: the two readings of vasyam (dwelt in / clothed) are given voice. Confirm that Shankara glosses vasyam as acchadaniyam, 'to be covered', and that the 'dwelt in' reading is fairly attributed to 'readers' generally (no school named on purpose).
'Readers have been hearing it two ways for a long time' is general; soften to 'readers hear it two ways' if a Keeper prefers.
Grammar to confirm: isha as the instrumental of the stem ish ('by the Lord'); jagatyam as the locative of jagati ('in the moving world').
